options: Sputum microscopy and culture for acid-fast bacilli
set.explanation: Months of cough, fever, night sweats and weight loss with bilateral upper-zone shadowing in a diabetic patient is pulmonary tuberculosis until proved otherwise. At least 2–3 sputum samples (one early-morning) for acid-fast bacilli smear and mycobacterial culture confirm the diagnosis and give drug sensitivities; a rapid molecular test (e.g. Xpert MTB/RIF) is run on the same sample where available. FBC, ESR and CRP are non-specific, a tuberculin skin test cannot separate latent from active disease, and bronchoscopy with lavage is kept for patients who cannot produce sputum or are smear-negative.

why: Nucleic acid amplification test replaced by tuberculin skin test: WHO recommends a rapid molecular test on sputum as an initial test, so two options were defensible

set.explanation: Jaundice appearing weeks after starting rifampicin, isoniazid and pyrazinamide is drug-induced hepatotoxicity until proved otherwise; it is commonest in the first 2 months and more likely in older, malnourished or alcohol-using patients or those with liver disease. If ALT rises above 5 times normal or bilirubin rises, the hepatotoxic drugs are stopped and, once liver tests normalise, reintroduced one at a time under monitoring. Viral hepatitis should be excluded with serology, but the timing points to the drugs, and gallstone disease or cirrhosis would give a different clinical and biochemical picture.

set.stem: A 25-year-old woman with diabetes has had cough, fever, night sweats and weight loss for 4 months. She has finger clubbing and crackles over both apices; the chest X-ray shows ill-defined opacities in both upper zones. Risk factors for tuberculosis are grouped into patient-related factors and associated diseases. Which of the following is an associated disease rather than a patient-related factor?
options: Close contact with a smear-positive case
Chest X-ray evidence of self-healed tuberculosis
set.explanation: Diabetes mellitus is one of the associated diseases that impair cell-mediated immunity and raise the risk of reactivation, together with HIV infection, immunosuppressive drugs (corticosteroids, anti-TNF agents), chronic kidney disease, silicosis, malignancy, gastrectomy or malabsorption, vitamin A or D deficiency and recent measles in children. Overcrowding, smoking, close contact with a smear-positive case and radiological evidence of old healed tuberculosis are patient-related (exposure and host) factors. Diabetic patients with tuberculosis need tight glycaemic control, and rifampicin lowers the levels of sulfonylureas.

why: Original options held four 'associated diseases' (CKD, diabetes, silicosis, vitamin A deficiency) against the key's own classification; stem and distractors rewritten so diabetes is the single best answer

set.explanation: Most patients with pulmonary tuberculosis are treated as outpatients. Admission is justified when the diagnosis is uncertain, when drugs are not tolerated (severe gastrointestinal upset, hepatotoxicity), when adherence is doubtful or social circumstances are poor, when the patient is seriously ill, or when drug resistance is suspected or proved (multidrug-resistant tuberculosis needs isolation in a negative-pressure room). Diabetes increases the risk of tuberculosis and needs good glycaemic control but is not in itself a reason to admit.

Drug resistance arises from inadequate treatment: poor-quality drugs, drug shortages, poor prescribing and health-care provision, lack of supervision (no directly observed therapy) and non-adherence, so previous treatment or treatment failure is the strongest predictor; resistant strains can then be transmitted to contacts. Diabetes raises the risk of developing tuberculosis but is not a cause of drug resistance. Every new case should have rapid molecular testing for rifampicin resistance (e.g. Xpert MTB/RIF).

set.stem: A 76-year-old man has fever, productive cough and worsening breathlessness for 2 days and is confused. T 39.1°C, BP 92/58 mmHg, RR 32/min, HR 122/min, SpO2 88% on air. Serum urea 12.1 mmol/L (BUN 34 mg/dL), WBC 18 × 10⁹/L, lactate 3.1 mmol/L; the chest X-ray shows bilateral multilobar infiltrates. What is the most appropriate disposition?
set.explanation: His CURB-65 score is 5 (confusion, urea above 7 mmol/L, respiratory rate 30/min or more, diastolic BP 60 mmHg or less, age 65 or over), which predicts a 30-day mortality above 40%, and he also has multilobar disease, hypoxaemia and a raised lactate indicating sepsis. BTS guidance is to manage a CURB-65 score of 4–5 as high-severity pneumonia with early critical-care review, IV co-amoxiclav plus clarithromycin, oxygen and fluids. Ward care is for moderate severity (score 2), and home treatment is only for a score of 0–1.

why: Same idea as resinf-0001 (suspected pulmonary tuberculosis vignette: sputum for AFB smear and culture is the key test)

set.stem: A 39-year-old man started standard four-drug treatment (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) for pulmonary tuberculosis 2 weeks ago. He now has abdominal pain, fatigue, dark urine and mild jaundice, and an acutely painful, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint. AST 220 U/L, ALT 260 U/L, ALP normal, bilirubin 53 µmol/L (3.1 mg/dL), serum urate 0.62 mmol/L (raised). Which drug is most likely responsible for both problems?
set.explanation: Pyrazinamide causes dose-related hepatocellular injury and also blocks renal urate excretion, so hyperuricaemia and acute gout alongside a hepatitic liver profile point to it. Isoniazid is the other common cause of hepatitis (with peripheral neuropathy, prevented by pyridoxine) but does not cause gout, rifampicin tends to cause a cholestatic picture and orange secretions, and ethambutol causes optic neuritis. The hepatotoxic drugs are stopped until liver tests settle and then reintroduced sequentially, often without pyrazinamide.

why: Isoniazid and pyrazinamide were equally defensible for isolated hepatitis; hyperuricaemic gout added to the stem so pyrazinamide is the single best answer

set.explanation: Daily purulent sputum, recurrent pneumonia, haemoptysis and coarse crackles suggest bronchiectasis, and high-resolution CT confirms it by showing airways wider than the accompanying artery (signet-ring sign), lack of tapering and bronchi visible near the pleura. A chest X-ray is often normal or shows only tram-lines, sputum culture identifies colonising organisms (Haemophilus, Pseudomonas) but not the structural diagnosis, and bronchoscopy is kept for focal disease or suspected obstruction. Once confirmed, BTS guidance advises tests for a cause (immunoglobulins, ABPA serology, CF and ciliary testing where appropriate).

Rising PaCO2 in pneumonia means the patient is tiring and can no longer maintain ventilation, a recognised BTS indication for intensive care assessment, along with persisting hypoxia despite high-flow oxygen, severe acidosis, shock and reduced consciousness. A CURB-65 score of 2 is moderate severity, managed on the ward. Respiratory alkalosis from tachypnoea is expected in early pneumonia, and the organism alone (e.g. Haemophilus influenzae) does not decide the level of care.

Primary tuberculosis is often a mild flu-like illness, and the hypersensitivity reaction as the tuberculin test becomes positive may cause erythema nodosum or phlyctenular conjunctivitis; the chest X-ray may show a Ghon focus with hilar nodes. Erythema marginatum belongs to rheumatic fever, finger clubbing reflects chronic suppurative lung disease or cancer rather than early infection, and hepatomegaly is not a typical sign of primary infection.

Heavy drinkers are at risk of aspirating oropharyngeal anaerobes; after 1–2 weeks this produces a lung abscess with swinging fever, foul-smelling sputum, finger clubbing and a thick-walled cavity with an air–fluid level, typically in dependent segments (right lower lobe). Treatment is prolonged antibiotics with anaerobic cover (e.g. co-amoxiclav, or a beta-lactam plus metronidazole) and postural drainage. Tuberculous cavities are usually apical with a slower course, COPD exacerbations and pulmonary emboli do not produce foul sputum and a fluid-filled cavity.

Primary tuberculosis can cause hypersensitivity manifestations such as erythema nodosum and phlyctenular conjunctivitis, and in children tuberculous dactylitis of the short bones of the hand. Erythema marginatum is a transient, ring-shaped rash on the trunk that is a major Jones criterion for acute rheumatic fever and is not a feature of tuberculosis.

set.stem: A patient with acute lobar pneumonia has herpes labialis (cold sores). Which organism is the most likely cause of the pneumonia?
set.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the commonest cause of community-acquired and lobar pneumonia, and the fever it causes often reactivates latent herpes simplex as cold sores; rusty sputum and pleuritic pain are other classic features. Mycoplasma causes a patchy atypical pneumonia in young adults, Haemophilus influenzae usually infects patients with COPD, and Staphylococcus epidermidis is a skin commensal and line contaminant rather than a lung pathogen.

why: Cervical lymphadenopathy is not a recognised clue to pneumococcal pneumonia; replaced by herpes labialis, the classic association

options: Rapid molecular test on sputum (Xpert MTB/RIF)
set.explanation: IGRA (like the tuberculin skin test) detects T-cell sensitisation to M. tuberculosis and cannot distinguish latent from active infection; in a high-prevalence country many healthy adults are positive, so it adds little to the diagnosis of active disease and is used mainly to screen for latent infection before immunosuppression. Chest X-ray, sputum smear and culture, and WHO-recommended rapid molecular tests such as Xpert MTB/RIF, which also detects rifampicin resistance within hours, are the tests that diagnose active pulmonary tuberculosis.

why: Mantoux test replaced by Xpert MTB/RIF: the Mantoux test is equally unhelpful for active TB, so two options were correct

set.explanation: For moderate-severity pneumonia (CURB-65 score 2) NICE and BTS recommend amoxicillin, with clarithromycin added when atypical cover is needed; in penicillin allergy, doxycycline or clarithromycin alone is used. Meropenem is reserved for hospital-acquired or resistant infections, gentamicin has poor activity against pneumococcus, and ceftriaxone carries a small risk of cross-reactivity and is not first choice in moderate pneumonia.

Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia, often following influenza or in injecting drug users, is necrotising and frequently bacteraemic, so it can seed metastatic abscesses in the brain, bone, joints or heart valves as well as cause lung abscess, pneumatocoeles and empyema. Pneumococcal pneumonia can cause meningitis but rarely abscesses, and Mycoplasma, Legionella and Pseudomonas are not typical causes of brain abscess.

Patient-related risk factors for tuberculosis include age (the risk is highest in young children and the elderly, lowest in young adults), close contact with a smear-positive case, overcrowding, smoking, first-generation migration from high-prevalence areas and chest X-ray evidence of old healed tuberculosis. Being aged 20–25 years is not in itself a risk factor. Associated diseases such as HIV, diabetes, CKD and silicosis form the second group of risk factors.

The tuberculous granuloma is a cell-mediated (type IV) response: activated macrophages become epithelioid cells and fuse into Langhans giant cells with a horseshoe of nuclei, surrounded by lymphocytes and fibroblasts, often with central caseous necrosis. Neutrophils belong to acute suppurative inflammation and are not a characteristic component of the granuloma.

why: Same idea as resinf-0001 (chronic constitutional symptoms with upper-zone shadowing: sputum for AFB is the key investigation)

set.explanation: Weeks of fever, night sweats and weight loss with haemoptysis in a young adult is classic pulmonary tuberculosis; bleeding comes from cavities or eroded bronchial vessels (rarely a Rasmussen aneurysm), and sputum for AFB is the next step. Acute pneumonia lacks the constitutional course, haemophilia rarely causes haemoptysis without trauma, and granulomatosis with polyangiitis would usually show nasal, sinus or renal involvement.

why: Same idea as resinf-0003 (distinguishing associated diseases such as diabetes from patient-related factors such as overcrowding)

set.explanation: Sputum for acid-fast bacilli (Ziehl–Neelsen or auramine smear, with rapid molecular testing) and mycobacterial culture is the key test because it confirms active disease, shows infectiousness and provides drug-sensitivity results; culture remains the gold standard. The tuberculin skin test and IGRA only show sensitisation and cannot separate latent from active disease, and the chest X-ray is suggestive but not diagnostic.

why: Same idea as resinf-0005 (causes of drug-resistant TB; diabetes is the odd one out)
Same idea as resinf-0004 (indications for hospital admission in tuberculosis)

set.explanation: Reduced expansion, dullness, bronchial breathing and reduced air entry confined to one zone, with fever and purulent sputum, are the signs of lobar consolidation. Bronchopneumonia gives patchy bilateral crackles rather than signs of lobar consolidation, and acute bronchitis, COPD and asthma cause wheeze without dullness or bronchial breathing.

Streptococcus pneumoniae causes about a third to a half of community-acquired pneumonias where a pathogen is found and is the classic cause of lobar consolidation. Haemophilus influenzae is typical in COPD, Klebsiella in alcohol users (upper-lobe cavitating disease), Staphylococcus aureus after influenza, and Mycoplasma gives a patchy atypical picture in younger patients.

Low-severity pneumonia (CURB-65 score 0–1; here age alone scores 1) is treated with oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days, according to NICE and BTS guidance, with doxycycline or clarithromycin if the patient is penicillin-allergic. Ceftriaxone is an IV agent for more severe disease, metronidazole covers only anaerobes, and a macrolide alone is kept for allergy or suspected atypical infection.

Chronic productive cough, finger clubbing and male infertility suggest bronchiectasis due to a condition that also affects the vas deferens or sperm, such as cystic fibrosis (congenital absence of the vas), primary ciliary dyskinesia (immotile sperm, Kartagener syndrome with situs inversus) or Young syndrome. Sarcoidosis and chronic bronchitis do not cause clubbing or infertility, and cyanotic congenital heart disease causes clubbing but not a productive cough or infertility.

why: Garbled copy of the same question as resinf-0017 (brain abscess complicating staphylococcal pneumonia)

set.stem: A 40-year-old man with early right lower-lobe pneumonia has arterial blood gases on air: PaO2 8.1 kPa (61 mmHg), PaCO2 4.2 kPa (32 mmHg). Why is he hypoxaemic without hypercapnia?
options: Increased ventilation of healthy alveoli removes CO2 but cannot add extra oxygen to blood leaving the consolidated lung
Supplemental oxygen suppresses carbon dioxide production
The infection is too mild to affect gas exchange
Consolidation increases the diffusing capacity for carbon dioxide
set.explanation: Consolidated alveoli are perfused but not ventilated, so blood leaving them is both desaturated and CO2-rich. The raised respiratory drive increases ventilation of the healthy lung; because the CO2 content curve is almost linear, overbreathing normal units lowers their CO2 enough to compensate, whereas haemoglobin in those units is already nearly fully saturated and cannot carry extra oxygen, so type 1 respiratory failure results. A rising PaCO2 later in pneumonia signals exhaustion and is an indication for critical-care review.

why: Garbled stem (answer written into the question) rewritten as a stand-alone blood-gas question with rebuilt option wording
Same question as resinf-0018 (patient-related TB risk factors; age 20–25 is the odd one out)
